title: A Mother's Secret: Love & Sacrifice
subtitle: Learn English Through Stories • Level 2 Graded Reader
description: Linda lived alone in a quiet house in Ohio. Her son moved far away and grew busy, but in a small oak box beneath her bed lay a treasure that money could never buy.
dedication: Dedicated to every mother whose silent sacrifices paved the way, and to every child who remembers to call.

pages.title: A Grandmother's Quiet House
prose: My name is Linda Parker. I am 64 years old. I live alone in a small house in Ohio, USA. My husband died 10 years ago. I have only one son. His name is Daniel. He is 35 years old. He is married and has a little daughter named Emma. Emma is my only granddaughter. She is 7 years old. She has the same blue eyes as her father.

Every Sunday, I used to cook her favorite food. She loved my apple pie. Whenever she visited me, she would run into my arms and say, 'Grandma, I missed you.' Those were the happiest moments of my life.

But things changed after Daniel got married. At first, he called me everyday. Sometimes he visited me after work. He always asked if I needed anything. But slowly, his visits became less common. First he stopped coming every weekend. Then he started calling only once a week. And after some time, even those calls became very short. I tried not to complain. I knew he had his own family and many responsibilities.

vocab.meaning: Duties and tasks you are expected to take care of.
Happening rarely or not frequently.
The daughter of one's son or daughter.

pages.title: The Unexpected Announcement
prose: One evening, Daniel came to my house with his wife, Sarah. They sat in the living room. I made coffee for them and brought some cookies. But Daniel looked different that day. He was not smiling.
'Mom, we need to talk,' he said. I sat beside him. 'Of course, dear. What happened?' He looked at Sarah before speaking. 'Mom, we are moving to another city. I got a new job and it pays much better.'

I smiled. 'That's wonderful, Daniel. I am so happy for you.' But then he said something I was not ready to hear: 'We are leaving next week.' I looked at him. 'Next week? So soon?' 'Yes, Mom. We have already found a house.' I looked at little Emma who was playing with her doll on the floor. 'What about Emma? Will I still get to see her?' Daniel looked down. 'Of course, Mom. We'll visit whenever we get time.'

I wanted to ask him to stay. I wanted to tell him that this house would feel empty without them, but I did not want to hold him back. 'Of course, sweetheart, I understand.' Before leaving, Emma hugged my legs: 'Grandma, will you come to my new house?' I kissed her forehead: 'Of course, sweetheart, I promise.' I did not know that it would become a very difficult promise to keep.

vocab.meaning: To restrain or prevent someone from progressing.
Provides a significantly higher income/salary.
A sincere assurance that one will do something.

pages.title: The Distance & The Growing Silence
prose: The next week, Daniel and his family left. I stood outside my house and watched their car disappear down the street. I kept waving until I could no longer see them. Then I went inside. The house was silent. No little girl running through the hallway. No Daniel asking what was for dinner. No voices. Just me and the ticking clock on the wall. That night, I cooked dinner for one person for the first time in many years. I made Daniel's favorite chicken soup, but I could not eat it. I sat at the kitchen table and cried.

Daniel had promised to call, and he did. For the first few weeks, he called every Sunday. He told me about his new job, his new house, and Emma's school. I loved hearing about their lives, but slowly the calls became shorter. Sometimes he said he was busy, sometimes he said Emma was sleeping, and sometimes he did not answer at all. I started calling less because I did not want to disturb him.

One Sunday, I waited near the phone from morning until evening. He never called. When I finally called him at 9 PM, he answered: 'Mom, I'm really busy. Can we talk tomorrow?' I became quiet. 'Of course, dear. Take care.' He ended the call. I looked at the family photograph beside my bed. 'I miss you, sweetheart,' I whispered.

vocab.meaning: To cease to be visible; vanish.
To interrupt or bother someone while they are busy.
Spoke in a very soft, quiet voice.

pages.title: The Secret Wooden Box
prose: Three months passed. Winter arrived in Ohio. The streets were covered with snow and the cold wind came through the small gaps in my windows. Sometimes my neighbor, Mrs. Wilson, came to visit me. 'Linda, why don't you visit your son?' she asked. I smiled: 'He's busy with work. I don't want to trouble him.' She looked at me sadly: 'Linda, you are his mother. You are not a trouble.' I did not answer.

A few days later, while cleaning my bedroom, I found an old birthday card Daniel had given me when he was only 10 years old. Inside he had written: 'Dear Mom, when I grow up, I will buy you a big house. You will never have to work again. I will take care of you just like you take care of me. Love, Daniel.'

As I closed the drawer, I noticed something behind it: a small wooden box. It was old and covered with dust. Inside that box was the one thing I had never told Daniel about: several envelopes, a notebook, and a bank book. On the first envelope was written: 'For Emma on her 18th birthday.'

When Emma was born, I made a promise to save for her future. Every month, I put money aside—$20, $50, or whatever I earned from my sewing work. I never bought expensive clothes or went to restaurants. I even sold old jewelry. I had opened a savings account in Emma's name and written letters for each milestone birthday so she would know how much her grandmother loved her.

vocab.meaning: An inconvenience or burden to others.
A significant stage or event in the development of something.
Joining or mending clothes using a needle and thread.

pages.title: A Silent Birthday & The Bank Call
prose: A week later, my birthday arrived. I turned 65. I woke up early and made myself a cup of tea. I waited until noon. Nothing. At 3:00 in the afternoon, I finally received a text message from Daniel: 'Happy birthday, Mom. Sorry, I am busy today. We will talk soon.' I read it twice. Then I typed, 'Thank you, son. I love you.' I waited for a reply, but nothing came. Mrs. Wilson brought a small cake and sang with me, but after she left, I sat alone in the living room wondering if my son would ever return.

Two more months passed. One morning, an unknown number rang. 'Hello, Mrs. Parker. My name is James from the bank. I am calling about a savings account you opened for your granddaughter Emma. We just need to confirm a few details. Would you like us to send the account information to your son as well?'

I thought for a moment: 'No, please. I want to speak to him myself.' After ending the call, I looked at the wooden box under my bed. I knew it was time. I picked up my phone and called Daniel: 'Daniel, I need you to come home.' He sounded worried: 'Mom, what happened? Can it wait? We are very busy this week.' I closed my eyes: 'No, Daniel, please. I don't know how much longer I can wait.' There was silence. Finally, he said, 'Okay, Mom. I will come this Saturday.'

vocab.meaning: To establish the truth or correctness of something.
Complete absence of sound or speech.
Feeling or inspiring optimism about future events.

pages.title: Opening the Letters
prose: Saturday arrived. I cleaned the house, made Daniel's favorite chicken soup, and baked an apple pie for Emma. At 2:00 PM, a car pulled into the driveway. It was Daniel, Sarah, and Emma. Emma ran inside: 'Grandma! I missed you so much!'

I brought the wooden box and placed it on the kitchen table in front of Daniel. 'Open it, son.' He lifted the lid and found the envelopes, the notebook, and the bank book. Daniel opened an envelope and read: 'Dear Emma, if you are reading this, you are now 18 years old. I hope you are happy and brave. I saved something for your future so you could follow your dreams. Love, Grandma Linda.'

Daniel's eyes welled with tears. He opened the bank book and saw more than $18,000 saved. 'Mom, how did you save all this money? Why didn't you tell me?' I held his hand: 'Because I didn't want you to feel bad. I knew you had your own family to care for. I wanted to help Emma without making you worry.'

vocab.meaning: Filled up and began to spill over (with tears).
Ready to face danger or pain; courageous.
A bank account that earns interest on deposited funds.

pages.title: The Letter to Daniel
prose: At the bottom of the box was one last envelope: 'For my son Daniel. Open this when you are ready.' Daniel opened it with trembling fingers:

'Dear Daniel, do you remember the small house where you grew up? Do you remember the winter when your father lost his job? You were only 8 years old. You woke up and asked why I wasn't sleeping. The truth was that I had skipped dinner so there would be enough food for you. I never wanted you to feel poor; I wanted you to feel loved.

When you moved away, I missed you every day. But I never wanted you to give up your happiness just to take care of me. One day, Emma will grow up with her own dreams and family, and perhaps one day she will also be too busy to visit. When that day comes, do not be angry with her. Just love her. That is all a parent can do. Love, Mom.'

A tear fell onto the paper. Daniel covered his face and wept: 'Mom, I am so sorry. When I was young, you were always there for me. But when you needed me, I was not there for you.' I touched his cheek gently: 'You are here now, son.'

vocab.meaning: Shaking involuntarily with emotion.
Passed over or omitted doing something (like a meal).
Cried deeply with tears.

pages.title: The Greatest Wealth & Coming Home
prose: Then little Emma reached into her backpack: 'Grandma, I have something for you too.' She handed me a drawing of a small house with a woman, a little girl, and a man holding hands, titled 'My Family.' 'Daddy said we might move back near you one day,' she smiled.
Daniel looked at his daughter, then looked at me: 'Mom, I don't want you to spend another winter alone. We can find a house closer to yours. I want Emma to grow up with her grandmother.'
He shook his head: 'Mom, you were never a problem. I just forgot how important you are.' That evening, we ate dinner together, and the house was filled with warmth and laughter once again.

After they left, I looked at the oak box. The greatest thing I had saved was never the money—it was the love I had never stopped giving. A mother never asks for luxury or expensive gifts; all she wants is a little time, a phone call, and knowing she is remembered. If your parents are still with you, don't wait for a special day to call them.

vocab.meaning: A state of great comfort and extravagant living.
An abundance of valuable possessions, money, or love.
Of great value; not to be wasted or treated carelessly.
